Mr. Chairman, in my brief remarks last evening I was speaking on the question of possible railway line abandonments. Following the direction of Mr. Speaker, having read Hansard this morning perhaps I could just correct two names which appear at page 1059. What I said was that one line runs from Ferrona; it is printed in Hansard as Vernal. This line runs from Ferrona to Sunnybrae.
Then Hansard says that this is the old line built by the old Nova Scotia Railway Company. That should read the "Nova Scotia Steel Company". This line was taken over by

the "Inter-Colonial Railway"; Hansard records this as the "Colonial". There is an old saying in the maritime provinces-I do not know whether I am paraphrasing it correctly-that there were three things we were sure of-living, dying and having a ride on the old I.C.R.
With regard to these proposed abandonments I should like to say that with the introduction of the $50 million Scott Paper mill in the Pictou county area I hope this short line railway will not be closed down. A spur line has been built to this plant which will connect with the short line, and it is very important to the area to continue the railway connection as is. At one time these railway fines were not used as much as they could have been, though we are now getting out of the troubles which we were in. Undoubtedly Canadian National Railways will have some figures in this regard, but with the present economic upsurge in the area I would hope that no abandonment of this line will be carried out.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
Another matter is this. After reading the press I was advised that an agreement has been reached on special rates between the Scott Paper Company, Scott (Maritimes) Limited, and the C.N.R. for transportation of pulpwood to the United States. This means there is all the more reason to continue the operation of the present short fine running from Stellarton to Oxford Junction.
Another matter which I took up with the vice president of the Atlantic region, Mr. Grayston, not long ago was the operation of the express and freight facilities in Stellarton. The service there has been very poor. I was advised by the vice president that this matter would be looked into and a study made as a result of which a decision would be reached in the new year. I intend to pursue this matter further before the committee on transport. Undoubtedly the officials of the C.N.R. will be appearing before that committee.
I was pleased to note that the Minister of Transport in his release of December 13 announced there would be an integrated study of Atlantic provinces transportation problems. The minister stated in the last paragraph of that press release:
The study will consider the effectiveness of present transportation in the Atlantic provinces, bearing in mind the existing obligations of the federal government under the terms of union with Newfoundland, the Maritime Freight Rates Act and the general policy of the federal government to foster the economic development and well-being of the Atlantic region.
February 11, 1966

This subject was further pursued by my hon. friend from Saint John-Albert when he raised the question in the house not long ago. On that occasion he asked the minister whether the rights of the maritimes would be upheld in the legislation to be put before the house. The minister advised my hon. friend that this would be done. We are looking with a great deal of anticipation to the results of the study which has been set up by the minister. I understand that well known firms are involved. I trust that whatever comes forward will be brought before the house and that we will be able to discuss this vital matter of transportation in our area.
Another matter I should like to raise at this time concerns the Canadian coastguard. I have a question on the order paper in this regard. I am bringing forward these individual matters now rather than on specific items so the minister can reply on a later occasion.
The hon. gentleman made an announcement on May 27, 1965 to the effect that four additional vessels would be constructed to engage in this vital work of providing coast guard facilities in the Atlantic area. We know these vessels are urgently needed. I asked in my question whether the tenders would be regional or national. I should like to know this. In the past, during the days when we were sitting on the other side of the house, coast guard vessels of medium size were built and at that time we were able to construct one in the Ferguson yard in my constituency. The Minister of Transport of that day arranged that the contracts could be awarded regionally, though on a tender basis. I hope the minister will tell us when these new vessels will be constructed and when tenders will be called.
There is another matter of importance to the Atlantic area on which I wish to say a word or two. It concerns shipbuilding subsidies. I recall that a few years ago when Mr. Alex Watson was chairman of the maritime commission he was very anxious to set up a program of shipbuilding subsidies. I remember talking this over with him many times when I visited his office. He was instrumental in setting this up, and I wish to pay tribute to him at this time. The work he did will certainly be a memorial to him.
The intention of the original program was, of course, to assist our shipyards and the workers employed in them to compete with yards in other parts of the world. I enter this caveat about the present plan, having read
Supply-Transport
the minister's statement and noted the questions which have been asked in the house regarding it. My hope is that this 25 per cent subsidy sliding to 17 per cent in 1972 will be sufficient. Some shipyard officials are a little doubtful about this. We must watch it carefully.
There is one specific question I should like to put to the minister, and perhaps he would look into this. He said in his statement, and I am quoting:
At the same time the ship construction drawback regulations which permit drawback of 99 per cent of customs duties paid on imported goods used in the original construction of ships are to be withdrawn except where they apply on military equipment.
I should like to ask the minister what will happen in cases where a shipyard has ordered certain components before January 1, 1966, and still has not received them. Suppose the keel has been laid and the ship is in the course of construction though the actual components needed from abroad have not been received. Will this arrangement apply in such a case, or must the parts have been landed in Canada before January 1? This is of special importance to areas such as mine where the trawler construction program is under way. The minister has given me an assurance that this program will be continued, that the 50 per cent rate will continue to apply to trawler construction.
I should like to know how long this subsidy is likely to be continued. These trawlers are much needed in our fishing industry, as has been pointed out by my hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg, and they have provided a lot of work in our area. We hope many more of these trawlers will be constructed and, as I say, we would like to know how long the present policy is likely to continue.
When the minister visited my constituency on a certain occasion in November he landed on a certain airfield. Now, I am always glad to have the hon. gentleman in my area; indeed, I am sure he was of assistance in getting me re-elected. The minister knows Trenton airport. Eastern Provincial Airways maintain a service there. Incidentally, I heard someone refer to E.P.A. as "Eastern Pick-ersgill Airways". I know nothing about that, but I do know that the vice president of that air line was in contact with the Chamber of Commerce in the New Glasgow area and advised its members that certain improvements would be made to Trenton airport. I should like to ask whether there are any

plans for such improvements and, if so, what these involve and when they are to begin.
There is one other matter I should like to raise. I have had correspondence with the minister about it and I must say I got quick reply to my inquiry about the Pictou Island Telephone Company. The government is now getting out of the telephone service. I should like to suggest once again that it might be possible to put into the supplementary estimates, or some other appropriate place, a small amount in respect of this company.
Pictou Island is a small island, five miles long and two miles wide. Some of its inhabitants move away to Pictou for the winter after the fishing season is over. Those who remain have no means of communication except for the telephone and what is known as "the flying padre". Mail is delivered twice a week by this small plane flying in and out. I would ask the minister again to take a hard look to see whether anything can be done along the lines I suggest. Fifty dollars a month is little enough to help provide essential communications for those hardy folk who carry out lobster fishing in the winter. As I say, their only means of communication apart from the telephone is this small plane which sometimes cannot make its run for weeks at a time.
This is vital and would assist the Pictou Island Telephone Company a great deal.
[DOT] (12:00 noon)
There is another question the minister has not heard much about, and that is the matter of television coverage. During the last election campaign the minister came to my area and said I was so well liked that my neighbours thought I should stay home. I did not hear him say it; I just read the press report, but I want to thank him for saying I am well considered by my neighbours. I think my record here in the last eight years assists me a bit, and I want to let the minister in on a little secret concerning how he can make a lot of friends in Pictou county. Many hundreds of my constituents have signed petitions, and the local Chamber of Commerce has been looking into the matter of television coverage from station CHCH, which is on the C.T.V. network, from Halifax.

We have two satellite stations, one in Anti-gonish and one in Charlottetown, which provide some local broadcasting, but mostly C.B.C. programs. As stated by the president of the New Glasgow Chamber of Commerce we are a captive audience, but we require a T.V. satellite from channel 5. I hope the proposed study by the cabinet committee of the Fowler commission report will not take long in order that the present freeze on new licences can be ended.
I have a friend, Mr. Chairman, a neighbour of mine, brought up in the same town as myself, which is about five miles away. I am worried about him because he is a great hockey and football fan. He tells me that in order to see hockey and football broadcasts over the C.T.V. network he has to travel to the town of Westville, five miles away, in the middle of the night. Some day he may drive his car over a bridge on his way home, but he is only one among the many who desire and believe they should have this necessary T.V. coverage.
I hope some of the questions I have raised will be answered by the minister when he replies later on, and I reserve the right to raise further matters on various items of the estimates. Mr. Chairman, while the
affairs and estimates of the Department of Transport are before us I should like to draw the minister's attention once again to a very important project awaiting attention in my part of the province of Ontario. I have spoken on this subject before, and I wish to speak about it again because of its transcendent importance to my area. I refer to the redevelopment of the lower Grand river from its mouth at Lake Erie up as far as Brantford, so that it may be used by pleasure craft.
The Grand river has been a navigable stream as far up as Brantford from the earliest recorded times. As such, I maintain that its development and maintenance as a navigable stream come under the jurisdiction of the federal government, and in particular of the Department of Transport.
If the river be deemed not navigable now, then I believe it to be a matter or subject of discussion which should come before a meeting of the federal and provincial authorities, that is to say between the government in Ottawa and the government of Ontario, and I
February 11, 1966

am pleased to have been advised not long ago by the minister that this is going to be done in the very near future.
The importance of this matter to the entire population living anywhere near the Grand river watershed cannot be exaggerated or overestimated. The Grand river, in its course across western and southern Ontario, is one of the majestic waterways of our country. In times past, ships on the great lakes made regular trips up the Grand river to Brantford. Going from Brantford to Buffalo by water was a trip regularly taken by many in years gone by, before the advent of the railways.
I am telling the committee right now that if this body of water, scenic from its source to its mouth, were restored to navigable use by pleasure craft it would be of inestimable value to one of the most heavily populated areas in Canada. Today people are having more leisure time than ever before, and will have even more leisure hours in the future. I am, of course, referring to the entire population, to the masses of the people. With this in view, the necessity of readily available recreational centres becomes important and even urgent.
I am referring to places to which ordinary people can resort for recreation in the afternoon or evening. A lot of money is being spent on parks, including wilderness parks, but I am referring to recreational areas accessible to metropolitan centres of population such as the heavily populated districts close to Hamilton and around what is called the golden horseshoe of Ontario. Hon. members know that the highways of western Ontario are crowded with automobiles and other vehicles hauling boats to the lakes and to Georgian bay. Boating has become a source of widespread interest to large sections of our population. For large numbers of them it would be unnecessary to haul their boats long distances when they could so easily put their craft afloat on the waters of the Grand river.
In the centre of my province, and close to the most thickly populated part of it, is the greatest potential area for boating in Canada. I am not referring to boating on the high seas but boating on a magnificent waterway unequalled in beauty from earliest times.
Millions and millions of dollars have been spent by the federal government on the Trent canal and waterway, and upon the Rideau river and waterway. Today I am asking the government to begin giving consideration to the Grand river. I am asking for this today

but before long, indeed before even a year has passed, all manner of representations will be made to the minister from many quarters, and all relating to this project. They will be coming from boards of trade and from the Grand river conservation authority. At this juncture I should like to quote from the Brantford Expositor of Tuesday February 8, 1966, which carries a report headed "Grand River Conservational Authority Bill Introduced in Ontario Legislature." It reads:
A bill to establish the Grand river conservation authority was introduced in the Ontario legislature Monday by Energy and Resources Minister Simonett.
The new authority will be a union of the Grand valley conservation authority and the Grand river conservation commission.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
It is proposed on a three year trial basis. The legislation makes allowance for restoration of the separate groups Jan. 1, 1969, if the merger is unsatisfactory.
I have said, Mr. Chairman, that representations will be coming from municipalities in the Grand river valley and from all manner of interested bodies of people and taxpayers. I am told that the Brantford and suburban planning board is asking the new Grand river conservation authority to acquire all the flood lands of the Grand river in Brantford township, in Brantford itself and at Paris, and that proposals are being made to the municipal authorities to create a boating course from the area near the Brantford Golf and Country Club to the Lome bridge dam by dredging the river. The municipality can do this with the help of the province and with the additional help of the federal government.
Recently officers of the urban renewal project at Brantford were asked by me over the air whether the Grand river figured in their plans, and I was advised over the air by these men that a renovation and restoration of the river was necessary and definitely within the scope of their plans.
I have stated that this-and I refer to the valley of the Grand-will become a great recreational area. It has the potential to become second to none in North America, and at the same time it could be a conservation area of great significance. The need for adequate supplies of water everywhere is a matter of concern to all governing bodies today, and here we have one of the greatest sources of pure fresh water available for many uses, that can be found anywhere and, assuredly, close to the centres of population.

A number of years ago the city of Brantford, pursuant to new provincial regulations, installed a new sewage disposal plant, putting an end for all time to the dumping of raw sewage into the Grand river, that most beautiful body of water. Other municipalities have followed suit, and the Grand river today is being returned to the beautiful stream it once was. The municipalities have been doing their part; the provincial authorities have been doing their part and we are now looking to the federal authority to do its part in respect of this important matter.
Mr. Chairman, I do not hesitate to ask the minority Liberal government to take hold of this matter. I do not believe this house would begrudge any expenditure for this purpose, because I believe that in this chamber we have a lot of very big men today; we have a lot of men and women who take a big view of our country and, no matter what part of Canada they represent, I know they would be only too happy if some of us who come from what we like to call the banner province of this country want to push this province ahead within our confederation.
Mr. Chairman, the installation of low dams at one or two necessary points and the development and reinforcement of the dam at Caledonia, Ontario, would effectively hold back water to the enormous benefit of the agricultural areas on each side of the Grand river, and to the benefit as well of the large sections of the population nearby in the improved facilities for boating. Did you know that in the days before the 1860's people came all the way from the southern part of the United States, through the present inland waterway from Florida up to the Hudson river, across on the Erie canal to lake Erie and up to the Grand river to spend summers in the delightfully cool climate to be found at Brantford, Ontario? The Hotel Kirby and other hostelries were crowded in those days, and many of these visitors brought their slaves with them at that time.
Today in modern times, by the elimination of sewage outlets, the Grand river is being restored to its pristine beauty, and once again modern man in Ontario wants the Grand river back as it once was. It is becoming a challenge to this parliament and in particular to the Department of Transport, to create of it and around it a mighty potential recreational and conservational area.
I must say that I have been urging the Minister of Transport to commence a study of engineering costs of the development of the

Grand river for navigation for pleasure craft, a study to be entered into in conjunction with the provincial government. I am happy to say that the minister has received my representations not only cordially but with considerable interest.
The Grand river flows past the lands of the Six Nations Indian reservation, the home of that magnificent chief and ally of the British crown, Captain Joseph Brant. He and his advisers chose this locality as the heartland of a true British North America many, many years ago. It has both historical associations and current possibilities for our province and for the urban and rural residents of a great part of Ontario.
Mr. Chairman, I do not think I have been over enthusiastic about this project. If action is wanted there must be enthusiasm to bring it about. We have formed a Company of Young Canadians. Let the minority Liberal government lead them with enthusiasm into the Canada of the future. Is this not the essence of Liberalism, to give leadership in this regard? This is not in my view a government of tired old men; this is a government that can and should have a mind for the future, to create adequate areas of recreation close to the urban centres for the younger people, for the heads of families and for the older people as well, if only to sit on the banks and watch.
To my mind, as the Liberal member for Brantford, this project should be near the top of the agenda of projects to be sponsored by a forward looking government.

I wish to assure him now that if, one day-one never knows the designs of Providence-if I should hold a position of some responsibility, I would listen with special attention to any request he could then address to me.
Today, I am the one to call on his kind attention and urge him to show his utmost liberalism and liberality.
I would call the minister's attention on two points. First, on the increase in air traffic at Dorval during the World Fair and second, on the necessity of making operative to that end, the Sherbrooke airport which is situated in my area.
It has been established that the Dorval airport facilities will not meet Expo requirements. It is expected that, in 1967, there will be three times as many flights coming in daily from the United States alone. Dorval would be limited to the large jets, and St. Hubert airport would be used for additional facilities.
Transportation facilities must, therefore, be provided for within reasonable distance from Expo. The problems will not be limited solely to plane landings. Dorval airport will also be overcrowded with tourists and their baggage. That is why the minister must make immediate plans to improve air traffic and conditions in view of Expo '67.
The Sherbrooke airport, Mr. Chairman, is surely the answer to problems which are bound to arise. With the new two-year-old highway between Sherbrooke and Montreal, the Sherbrooke airport is only one and a half hour's drive to Expo grounds.
The airport is near the American border and air transportation, including helicopter service, will also be readily available to American tourists between Sherbrooke and Expo.
Since Montreal's hotel accommodation and restaurant facilities will surely not be able to cope with the demand, Sherbrooke and adjacent areas will offer good comfortable accommodation as an alternative. A number of other reasons would warrant the completion of Sherbrooke airport and show how important this airport is.
This Sherbrooke airport is fairly important. The minister will recall that it is located on high ground, and that it spreads on a plateau that is very favourable to air navigation.
It was built between 1959 and 1961, and it now includes-although initial plans call for a
Supply-Transport
greater number of runways-a 6,000 foot runway. It has a non-directional radio beacon and an aeronautical station. This work cost the government $1,221,564. An air terminal has just been completed at an additional cost of $115,000. Furthermore, the ground is ready for construction of another runway.
According to information given to the house on June 28, 1965-as recorded on page 2920 of the official report-the Sherbrooke airport can now accommodate DC-9's and could accommodate DC-8's and Boeing 707's, if the runway were 1,000 feet longer.
Consequently, my request to the minister is fourfold:
First, use the Sherbrooke airport as an adjunct to the Dorval airport to provide for the increased air traffic at the time of the world exhibition;
Second, as soon as it is convenient, grant credits to lengthen to 7,000 feet the existing runway, to enable DC-8 and Boeing 707 to land easily;
Third, study the need to build a second
7,000	foot runway.
Finally, pay to the city of Sherbrooke half the cost of the terminal, by increasing the grant from $26,709 to $57,500.
I ask the minister to review and increase the grant for the air terminal because, according to a statement made by the mayor of Sherbrooke, Mr. Armand Nadeau, Q.C., last December 21, 1965, the cubic measurements were miscalculated for the purposes of the grant.

A few days ago, Mr. Chairman, I was telling the Minister of Transport that I was going to endeavour to help him with his estimates. I believe at the time he misunderstood me, but I can assure him that the word I used was "help". I should like, in the few minutes I have at my disposal, to convey the minister on a tour of the Gaspe peninsula by means of the transportation facilities we have in that area. I know it is the lunch hour, but I am sure the minister would get a better sandwich back of the curtains than he would if he were to travel on the Canadian National system which we have in our area.
A region such as the Gaspe peninsula requires a transportation system that is efficient, regular and fast. The main concern must be that goods which are coming into the region and those that are going out must move at the cheapest rates possible. The economy of the peninsula is no longer one of fishing and lumbering only. Although the fishing industry is contributing substantially to our economy, there are fewer fishermen in the trade with a greater output as the result of technological and scientific advances in the trade.
Lumbering is also demanding fewer men, although the output is gradually increasing. There remains for us the tourist industry, the mining industry and manufacturing.

The population of the area demands the right to be assured a way of life equal to that of people in other areas of Canada. Our geographical position, our distance from populated areas of the province which form the large consuming centres, puts us in a rather unfortunate position. This results in our citizens having to pay more for their purchases and receiving much less for the goods they sell. This situation, Mr. Chairman, of course also has the effect of creating a reluctance on the part of the industry to come to the area.
How can some of these inconveniences be overcome? I am sure that to attain that goal we must first of all create a favourable climate for industry to come to the area. Transportation is our greatest problem. As I have said, this is the result of our geographical position and our distance from large consuming centres.
Let us look at some of the transportation facilities which we have in the area now. I will take the south coast of the riding or of the peninsula, and there we have a railroad completed in 1915, running from Matapedia to Gaspe. The facilities there today are, naturally, a freight service and a local train running the 200 miles. The local train carries one passenger car of the vintage of 1915, still with wooden benches and a coal stove in the corner of the car. The other passenger facility is a Budd car running from Gaspe to Matapedia daily. You may, if you are lucky, get aboard that train. Many, many times I have seen that train when passengers were unable to get aboard for some 50 or 70 miles because of the lack of seating capacity. However, it is better than nothing, and we have to travel by that system. You may also buy a sandwich on that train, even if the train is four, six or eight hours late. I think the sandwich is made in Montreal, sent to Campbellton and possibly a week later put aboard that railway car.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not believe the citizens of that area are any different from those in any other area? They are not, and will not be considered, second class citizens. We expect to have a transportation system equal to that which links Halifax and Montreal, the distance being about the same. I will endeavour to tell you how we are treated once we get to the main line. If you are one of those who come, say, a distance of 75 miles from Gaspe to board the train, you naturally have your meal at noon. Then you come to Gaspe and leave there at 2.30 in the

afternoon, arriving in Montreal the next morning at seven thirty or eight o'clock. In order to do this you must come by Budd car to Matapedia and there change trains, but not to the Ocean Limited that is coming from Halifax. You board another train which is made up at Campbellton, 15 miles from Matapedia. About 95 per cent to 98 per cent of the people who travel on the Chaleur and who go between Campbellton and Montreal are from the Gaspe peninsula. We have to take a train that is made up 15 miles from Matapedia and we must stay aboard that train.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that we are overlapping services there, and the services we are receiving are not the best. It seems to me logical that if 98 per cent of the people who travel on the Chaleur are from the peninsula, the train should run directly from Gaspe to Montreal. Why can we not have the same sleeping facilities as are on the Ocean Limited? Why can we not have the same meals as are available to those who travel on the Ocean Limited? We are paying the same prices; therefore we are entitled to the same services.
Now I am going to try, Mr. Chairman, to tell you what happens once you board that train called the Chaleur at Matapedia. You sit in the car which is probably of the 1925 or 1930 vintage. It is squeaky, and you do not sleep too well.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
However, perhaps you would like a meal before going to bed, having been on that train for six to eight hours. Occasionally there is a dining car on the train, though most of the time it is off. If boards of trade or public bodies complain they will put the dining car on; whenever criticism subsides then off comes the dining car.
When travelling on the Ocean Limited you sit down to a meal with a linen tablecloth on the table and you are given a linen napkin. But when you are a Gaspesian and you travel on the "Chaleur" you are given a place mat like the one I am holding in my hand. On it you read "Welcome. Good food and good service go together at C.N. Sit back, relax and put on your best appetite". Then it asks whether there is anything you need-a souvenir place mat, perhaps.
Would the hon. gentleman table that document?

I would be pleased to do so. I would also tell the minister that I picked it

up on the "Chaleur" on November 16, 1965. So you get a place mat free. But although I pay the same price as anyone coming from the maritime provinces, I am not entitled to a free meal on that train with my sleeping accommodation. They give me a menu which offers blended juice or soup and then you can have sandwiches; and I told you where the sandwiches usually come from. This train is made up at Campbellton; 20 minutes after the train leaves you look at the menu and choose a sandwich, but they tell you they are sorry, they have not any. As I say, the train left only 20 minutes before from its starting point in Campbellton, New Brunswick.

I object, as do all other Gaspesians, to the fact that we cannot get the same treatment as other people travelling the same distance going west to Montreal. I see the hon. member for Bona-venture sitting at his desk and I am sure he too is very aware of this problem and has made representations to the minister or to the C.N.R. Since he is now on the government side of the house I hope the minister will listen to him and try to put a little pressure on the C.N.R. to give the Gaspesians the service they deserve.
Now, in order to travel you must have money. In order to have money you must work. In order to work in the Gaspe peninsula you must have industry. In order to have industry you must have the encouragement of the government. It is no good doing what the Minister of Transport did a few years ago when there was an abatement in taxes across the country. In order to recover this money, the next day, he imposed additional wharfage charges on all goods on public wharves and also levied a tax on passengers crossing on ferries. This had the effect of paralyzing some of our industries.

Copper concentrate from that area goes to the smelting plant at Murdochville. Because we want all that concentrate to be smelted at Murdochville the government, being aware that this is a designated area and one needing government help, an area to which the attention of the government must be directed, imposed these special charges. I am sure that in one case, due to these extra wharfage charges, copper concentrate from

I am now going to the north side of my riding which, of course, the minister knows quite well, having heard a lot of debate in this house about a railroad which was supposed to be built in that section. Two former members of the cabinet went on a speaking tour in the Gaspe peninsula. One of them was the then Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. He made a speech about the money appropriated by act of parliament for construction of this railway. At one time he said the money was not voted, and the next time he said it was voted. at the Reform Club in Montreal, that the $7 million which will pay for the Riviere-du-Loup dock will be taken out of the $16 million earmarked for the north side of the Gaspe Peninsula. At an emergency

meeting, the Gaspe Chamber asked that Ottawa clear up once and for all the use of the $16 million.

On another occasion the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane made a speech about the $16 million which was intended for the construction of a railway between Ste. Anne des Monts and Matane. He said that-

-the $16 million which were intended to pay for the construction of a railroad between Matane and Ste. Anne des Monts will be used directly to benefit the areas concerned, that is to say the districts of Ste Anne des Monts and Cap Chat.

Now, Mr. Chairman, there is a contradiction somewhere, because that amount of money has not been spent on a railway between Ste. Anne des Monts and Matane. On August 5, 1964, as reported on page 6425 of Hansard, the minister said parliament had already recognized in principle the necessity for Ottawa to take steps to improve transport facilities in the Gaspe area. This 1 agree with. But further on, as reported on page 6426, the minister said:
It will be noted that the federal government does not intend to allocate the complete sum of $16 million to the road; we feel that part of this money could usefully serve for the development of airports and harbours which come under the direct jurisdiction of the federal government.
A number of plans for the development of harbours have been approved in principle and appropriate items will be entered in the supplementary estimates of the Department of Public Works.
Looking back over the estimates, and knowing the riding well, I believe there are two or three major projects which were to be undertaken immediately after that declaration by the minister. Not one of these projects has been carried out. At Ste Anne des Monts the money voted was intended for the repair of the wharf. Because of the bad state of repair of this wharf the ferry service between Ste. Anne des Monts and Sept lies has been discontinued, and any connection we have with the north shore of the St. Lawrence is by means of a detour through Matane. Had we developed Ste. Anne des Monts the people

of the peninsula would have been able to send goods to that area. If the railway had been built, goods could have been moved there more cheaply. But this government decided it would not spend the money on the railroad but that it would build a highway instead. Then instead of building it where they should have built it, they went outside the territory.
I should like the minister to clear up another ambiguity. Has any of this $16 million intended for the railway been used to undertake any other project in Quebec? We hear many rumours to this effect. In fact one of the hon. gentleman's colleagues formerly in the cabinet said it was the intention to build a deep water harbour at Riviere du Loup with some of this money. These are matters which are most ambiguous. We would like the minister to clear them up once and for all and tell us whether the money which was provided by act of parliament is still available. I have discussed our rail transportation system. I have discussed highway construction on the north side of my riding. I should now like to speak about air transportation. It is true that at this time we are undertaking some repairs to the Gaspe airfield. I refer again to the speech made by the Minister of Transport on August 5, 1964. He said then that the department had undertaken a survey of the peninsula in order to find a proper site for a district airport which would serve the main towns in the county of Gaspe.
I believe this is by no means an easy problem. If we are to build a district airport in the interior of Gaspe it is bound to involve a lot of expense. I believe it would be much better to improve the airfield at Gaspe, to build another at Chandler and a third in the region of Ste Anne des Monts-Cap Chat area. By so doing we would be covering the whole of the lower section of the peninsula. We might then be in a position to encourage travel by air and secure ready access to this whole area.

Apart from the Department of Public Works and the Department of Fisheries there is no federal department which touches the lives of my constituents as closely as does the Department of Transport. There are many matters I should like to deal with at this time, but in order not to unduly delay the passing of the estimates I will confine myself to one subject only, a subject which in my opinion is so urgent that I would be derelict in my duty to my constituents if I did not raise it at the very first opportunity.
Before I begin I should like to pay tribute to the officials of the Department of Transport, the officials of the minister's office, the senior officials and heads of branches in the head office here in Ottawa and to the district marine agent at St. John's. I should like publicly to express my gratitude to them for the sympathetic consideration they have always given to problems I have brought before them and for their all-out co-operation in trying to solve them.
The subject I wish to bring to the attention of the committee and of the government today is the urgent need for improvement in the C.N.R. coastal service in the western half of my riding. The constituency of Burin-Burgeo is made up of five provincial districts of which only one, the district of Burin, is accessible by road, and even this district is largely dependent on the C.N.R. coastal service for freight transportation. The other four provincial districts are completely dependent on the C.N.R. coastal service not only for transportation of freight but also for transportation of mail and passengers.
[DOT] (1:00 p.m.)
Of these four provincial districts, only Placentia West has a fairly satisfactory service based on the terminal at Argentia providing a frequency of two trips a week to all communities and three trips a week to the

February 11, 1986
Supply-Transport
larger ones. So far as the other three provincial districts are concerned the picture is vastly different. These three districts extend roughly along the south coast from Ter-renceville to Port aux Basques. This area is served by two C.N.R. coastal boats running between the western terminal at Port aux Basques and the eastern terminal at Argentia, with a weekly frequency in each direction. Except for the fact that these boats are slightly larger and the frequency of trips has increased from every 10 days to 7 days, this service is substantially the same as it was 50 years ago.
The coastline between Terrenceville and Port aux Basques contains some 50 communities with a total population of around 25,000, and it is mainly about the service to this area that I am complaining. On this strip of coastline there are located seven fresh fish processing plants and a number of supply firms and retail stores. All these enterprises are greatly handicapped by the slowness of the C.N.R. service upon which they are completely dependent.
Good, fast, reliable communications are a prime essential for the industrial development of any area, but the Canadian National Railway management think in terms of the nineteenth century. If they do not wake up soon the twentieth century will have completely passed them by without any substantial improvement being achieved. The population of this area about which I am speaking, between Terrenceville and Port aux Basques, has doubled since 1949, and the prosperity of the people has also increased. However, these two facts seem to have escaped the notice of the C.N.R. management.
We are living in the twentieth century and people do not want to spend a week travelling a distance that can and should be covered in a couple of days. Neither do they want to be delayed as they are now for hours and on some occasions for whole days by having to remain in port while the ship takes on and discharges cargo. Neither do they want to suffer the offensive odours and stench which emanate from cargoes such as fish meal, particularly during summertime when the weather is warm and people like to have their portholes open in order to enjoy the cool, fresh air.
Today people want to move as fast as possible. If they have two or three weeks holidays they want to spend the time with their friends and not travelling back and forth on the C.N.R. boats. Those who come

from long distances want to be sure of making connections with the air line services on which they have reservations for the return trip. None of these things are possible at present.
It has been obvious for years that the C.N.R. coastal service is terribly inadequate in terms of the amount of traffic to be handled. People from the United States and from mainland Canada who make their reservations months in advance often arrive at the Port aux Basques terminal only to find that the boat on which their reservations were made has been transferred to another route and the substitute boat provided does not have the type of accommodation they reserved.
Passengers are herded together in small rooms beneath deck or in small deck cabins so tiny that they have to put their luggage outside in order to be able to turn around. Dozens have difficulty in finding even a place to sit much less to lie down. Great credit is due to the crews of these boats; particularly to the captains, officers and stewards who quite often give up their own berths and go out of their way to do everything possible to alleviate the hardships and inconveniences to passengers inherent in these conditions. Without their sympathetic understanding and sacrifices the situation would be quite intolerable.
During the past two or three years I have written a number of letters about this matter to the C.N.R. and to the minister pointing out the deficiency in the service and suggesting remedies, but to date nothing has happened. Dealing with the Canadian National Railway is a most frustrating experience. You write a letter and you wait about two months. Then you get a reply saying they are looking into the problems involved in the matter you have raised. In about another two months you get another long letter defending their poor service. Their attitude seems to be that this service was good enough for our grandfathers and great-grandfathers and it should be good enough for people today.
When we try to pin them down they escape by saying, "Well, we do not own this railway in Newfoundland; we are only operating it for the federal government". Then when one approaches the federal government the answer is, "Well, we cannot do anything unless the C.N.R. management make a recommendation". Thus we go round and round in this vicious circle.

What is needed in my constituency is a completely new service based on twentieth century standards. This involves, first of all, separating the freight service from the passenger, mail and express service. Present boats could be utilized for scheduled freight service until more suitable and more economic boats can be obtained. Then they could probably be used in the summer for tourist trips to Labrador and in winter for tourist trips to the Caribbean and West Indies. For passengers, express and first class mail we need fast boats running between Port aux Basques and Terrenceville with a frequency of three trips a week each way.
I stress the fact that Terrenceville should be regarded as a terminal because it has been used as a passenger terminal for the past 12 or 14 years even though the eastern terminal is based at Argentia. There is no point in passengers staying on a ship for two or three days and travelling over rough waters when they can get to St. John's from Terrenceville by road within two hours.

of my employment in the transportation industry with the Canadian National Railways for the last 25 years. I must agree with the hon. member for Medicine Hat that many of the problems facing the industry today are a direct result of a lack of any comprehensive national transportation policy, a lack of delegation of authority and the improper exercise of the authority that does exist. It would appear that the Board of Transport Commissioners are not carrying out their proper function in protecting the interests of the public in respect of railway transportation. I think that one of the first questions one must ask is whether railway passenger service is a profitable enterprise. I must admit that the answer of necessity is that it is not an extremely profitable business. There are a great many more costly aspects involved in passenger transportation than in freight transportation. As an example of these extra costs let me point to the necessity of providing sleeping and dining facilities and the accompanying employment of sleeping car porters and dining car staff. In addition, there is always a possibility of a loss in respect of ordering foodstuffs. Public relations efforts must be maintained in order to induce people to travel by rail. In view of all the facts I have to admit that railway passenger service is not an extremely profitable enterprise.
It would appear from the Canadian Pacific's submission that the "Dominion" is not a profitable operation even during peak periods of business. I must disagree with that submission on this basis. Passenger service is not a profitable enterprise when looked at on a full time basis because there are peak periods and low periods. At times during low periods railway companies do only 20 per cent of the passenger business they do during peak periods. This makes passenger business a very precarious enterprise. However, during peak periods there must be a profit or the average loss would be a great deal higher.

The fact that there is a large number of Canadian box cars in the United States does not mean that there is a large number of grain cars there. The percentage of those cars used for transporting pulpwood and other rough materials is large. Some of them are used for transporting flour and such material. They are not grain cars and some of them would not be suitable for carrying grain. I would say that on the average 20 per cent to 30 per cent of those cars might be suitable for carrying grain.
The point I am trying to make is that it is not because we have so many cars in the United States on foreign lines that there is a shortage of grain cars. However, even though the problem I wish to talk about may not be a burning issue at the moment it could very well become contentious if action is not taken at the right time. I refer to the C.N.R. run-through program which was mentioned briefly a few moments ago.
The minister will recall the situation which developed in 1964 when the C.N.R. tried to institute run-throughs at Nakina and Wain-wright. Because of the action taken in this chamber and the strong representations made by the opposition, which were listened to sympathetically by the then minister, the government appointed Judge Freedman who made a very exhaustive report on the situation, which report was subsequently presented to the government. But up to the present we have no guarantee that the interested parties will tend to abide by the recommendations of Judge Freedman.
It would be some satisfaction to those of us concerned with this problem to get the minister's viewpoint. I am sure he is showing sufficient interest even at this moment to
February 11, 1966



enlighten the committee on the attitude which he feels should be taken in regard to this problem.

Mr. Chairman, in the best possible spirit, and without raising a technical point of order, may I venture to make a suggestion to the hon. member for Melville? I can give him an answer to one question. The railway does intend to have a conference with the unions on precisely the subjects mentioned in the Freedman report. I have been assured of that. Today the house leader told us that the estimates for all departments for the fiscal year 1966-67 will be tabled on Monday and I feel quite certain that this subject will still be a very active one when we reach the estimates for the forthcoming fiscal year.
I am not seeking to restrict the hon. member for Melville in any way but I was wondering whether members of the committee generally might think that subjects which could equally well be discussed on the 196667 estimates could be held over until we reach those estimates, thus allowing the committee to concentrate its attention at present on those things which hon. members feel would not be current after March 31. If hon. members feel that their speeches will have the same effect on the government after March 31 as before, then with a view to getting the whole business of the session through they might consider that suggestion.
Mr. Chairman, might I comment on the remarks of the minister apropos of the question? I simply wish to discuss his suggestion.

our remarks on the 1965-66 estimates when his friend, the hon. member for Brantford, was talking about the Company of Young Canadians, which has nothing to do with the Minister of Transport except that he himself might fit within that company.

Mr. Chairman, in regard to the minister's remarks let me say that I am sure none of us wishes to deny the fact that he has an engaging personality. It is true that when the estimates of the next fiscal year are referred to the appropriate committees a more detailed consideration will be undertaken than at this stage. However, I think the minister might be inclined to agree that there are a great many broad and varied fields coming within the general jurisdiction of his important department, and that by and large those who gave participated in the consideration of his estimates have done so in respect of broad policy issues. There has been no opportunity to deal with those issues because of a variety of circumstances upon which I will not enlarge at the moment.
It does seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that if the minister has a bit more patience and the members of the committee agree that this is the type of discussion we should have at this time, this will shorten considerably the consideration of transportation matters later this session.

Mr. Chairman, I am only a suppliant before the committee and it does not matter whether I agree. When I was on the other side of the house I often pointed out that ministers were only suppliants and I now know that much better than ever. However, you cannot blame me for trying.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to add a small contribution to this interesting discussion by stating that the minister should remember that it has been a long time since his department and many others have had a complete and thorough examination of their estimates. Mr. Chairman, I want to thank the minister for his very kind suggestion, and I do so with all sincerity. I have already achieved part of my purpose by bring-in this problem to his attention. Knowing the minister as I do, I am sure he will keep it in mind. I think he realizes, as all of us do, that the C.N.R. is going to proceed with these run-throughs. When they do the recommendations contained in this report should be taken into consideration. I hope that when this takes place in due course Judge Freedman's recommendations will be acted upon. With the minister's assurance that he will act in the most beneficial manner to all concerned I will defer any further remarks to a later time.
